desc: Stand straight, feet together, heels and toes touching. Weight evenly on both feet and along the whole length of each foot, toes lightly “holding” the floor. Shoulders broad, spine stretched up, head straight, gaze forward, arms relaxed along the body.

From the basic stance, smoothly extend the arms forward, palms down. Then, squatting slightly, sharply bend the elbows and pull the hands to the sides at the level of the solar plexus, turning the palms up on the way and slightly curling the fingers, as if drawing space toward you. A short, firm inhale of about a quarter of lung capacity.

The arms lower from the waist, then move smoothly forward and up parallel to each other, the gaze following the hands. When the arms are vertical, rise onto the toes and bring the gaze back forward. The arms go back, opening the chest: the arch is only in the thoracic spine, the lower back and neck lengthen up and forward without a kink.

Front view. On the whole foot, interlock the hands of the raised arms and turn the lock palms up, arms straightened to the limit. Slowly bend to the side — the point is not to compress one side but to stretch the opposite one. Hold the end position and smoothly straighten up.

From the exhausted thoracic half arch, lower onto the whole foot and bring the lower back and neck into the arch: first lengthen the spine, then arch. The navel goes forward and up, sternum up, crown back, straight arms in a reversed lock back and down. Belly slightly engaged, legs straight, no kink in the lower back or neck.

From the backbend, come forward in a wave from the pelvis, the legs stay completely straight. Torso, neck and arms extend into one horizontal line, hands locked. Pelvis tilted to the limit, sitting bones high, belly drawn in, the backs of the legs stretching.

The bend is a fold at the hip joints, not a rounding of the back. The pelvis tilts forward to the limit, the chest lies on the straight legs, the neck reaches with the crown toward the floor. The fingers of the straight arms press into the floor behind the feet through the work of the abs. At the end, rock slightly forward to stretch the hamstrings and Achilles tendons further.

In a deep bend, place the palms on the floor in front of the feet. Pushing with the arms and engaging the back muscles, arch so that you see the ceiling, while pressing the navel even closer to the thighs. Legs straight. One of the few poses where the movement is done on the inhale.

Closed bend with a grip: legs together and straight, take hold of the ankles and pull yourself down, lengthening the torso along the thighs. The chest presses to the legs, the spine “flows” freely down, the sitting bones reach up.

In a deep bend, interlock the straight arms behind the back, turn the lock out and lower the arms from behind the back forward and down, rotating the shoulders. The arms work as a lever: they help stretch the spine further down and press the belly to the thighs. Legs straight, sitting bones up.

Inclined plank: straight arms under the shoulders, the body in one straight line from heels to crown, supported on the toes and palms. Shoulders broad, feet shoulder-width apart or slightly wider, toes tucked under. Hold the position firmly.

From the inclined plank, reach the crown forward and up and roll over the toes onto the tops of the feet. The pelvis sags, the shoulders draw back and down, the spine stretches. Arms strictly straight — the wrists go into deep hyperextension. The movement is on the inhale.

From the sliding arched plank, in a wave, “spread” the body over an invisible plane a few centimetres above the floor. The elbows bend and press to the sides, shoulders drawn back, chest open, forehead and chin reaching forward.

Horizontal plank: the body parallel to the floor on bent arms, forearms pressed to the torso. Head, neck, torso, pelvis and legs form one horizontal line, supported on the toes. All muscles engaged; while holding, perform the “metal dog breath”.

From the horizontal plank, roll back, lift the pelvis and, engaging the back, arch in the thoracic spine. The sternum drops low but does not touch the floor, the head reaches forward and up without being thrown back. Picture a drawn bow before the shot.

On the inhale, “shoot” the torso up on straight arms. The shoulders open by rotating back and down, the whole body from toes to crown is one smooth arc with no kinks in the lower back or neck. Legs straight, knees pulled up, thighs engaged.

With a soft push, lift the pelvis up, the head drops between the arms. Feet on the floor shoulder-width apart, parallel, heels reaching toward the floor, legs straight. Pelvis tilted to the limit, back straight, arms and torso form one inclined plane. The body is like a mountain, with the sitting bones as its peak.

In the downward plank, on the inhale, arch back, “diving” the head forward and up. Palms and heels stay pressed to the floor, the body does not shift forward; at the same time the pelvis reaches back and up. The arch comes from the work of the back muscles.

On the exhale, lower the head and let it hang freely on a relaxed neck, ideally touching the floor. Shoulders slightly relaxed, everything else as in the downward plank. Relax all muscles not needed to hold the pose and breathe freely for one or two minutes.

From the downward plank, take a wide step forward, foot beside the hand. The pelvis lowers as far as possible, the front shin is vertical, the back leg is straight and on the toes, heel reaching back. Raise the torso vertically and, with a short firm inhale, pull the hands, palms up, to the waist.

In the wide step, slowly raise the arms forward and up and stretch into a backbend. The whole body is a flying arc from the back heel to the fingertips. Pelvis low and perpendicular to the thighs, the front thigh does not collapse inward. If confident, the hands can be joined in a reversed lock.

The head straightens, and on one slow full exhale spread the arms to the sides with tension. The hands are flexed back to the limit, index fingers straight, the other fingers bent. The depth of the element is set by the length of the exhale.

Lowering the arms, on the exhale arch even deeper, fingers reaching for the floor behind you. Bend the back leg as little as possible. All conditions of a safe backbend still apply: first lengthen, then arch.

The back knee lowers to the floor and the backbend becomes deeper still, the arms reaching for the floor behind. Pay special attention to the lower back — the thoracic spine does most of the work. Pelvis low, front thigh opened outward.
Return to the extended downward plank, but instead of placing one leg on the floor, lift it as high as possible back and up. The pelvis does not turn if possible, the supporting leg is straight.
From the three-point downward plank, lower the pelvis and stretch forward into the sliding arched plank, keeping the leg high and barely bending the knee.
The body straightens, the arms bend at the elbows, and we lower into a three-point horizontal plank. The raised leg stays up.

The pelvis rises, the head hangs freely and rests on the floor. The heel of the supporting leg is on the floor, the other leg is raised back and up, the pelvis does not turn. Arms and shoulders as in the deep downward plank.

Lowering the pelvis, come into an inclined plank with the head raised and, at the same time, bend the raised leg, drawing the knee in a circular movement from behind and above to the shoulder on the same side.

In the downward plank, the head rests on the floor at the border of the forehead and hairline; head, neck and back form one inclined straight line. Sitting bones up, heels on the floor. Join the straight arms behind the back in a reversed lock and reach the hands toward the floor beyond the head without disturbing the body position.

On all fours: palms by the head with fingers pointing straight forward, knees together or no wider than the feet, toes pointed. The chin reaches forward and up, the sitting bones back and up, shoulders drawn back, chest open. The arch comes from the back muscles.
Lengthening the spine, round the back upward in an arc. Chin pressed to the jugular notch, the muscles of the front of the torso engaged to the limit, the back relaxed and stretched.
From the arched cat, arch to the limit while extending one leg up and back. The pelvis and shoulder girdle stay horizontal and parallel.
Bend the raised leg and, in a circular movement from behind and above, draw the knee as close as possible to the ear on the same side.
Straighten the bent leg with tension, as if slowly delivering a roundhouse kick with the instep.
With a wide, slow circular swing, take the tensed leg back, reach it as high as possible and bend it, arching to the limit. Head raised.
Rise onto the toes of the supporting leg, round the back upward and draw the knee to the ear from below. Chin pressed to the jugular notch, the foot of the free leg does not touch the floor.
Slowly straighten the tensed leg forward and up beneath you, as if kicking with the instep. The heel does not touch the floor.
Bend the leg, draw the foot to the inside of the supporting thigh and, lowering onto the palms, slowly and with tension “kick” to the side with the outer edge of the foot.
Two-point support: with a circular swing, the leg goes back and up, the same-side arm extends forward and up. Head raised, chin reaching forward and up.
With the same-side hand, grip the ankle of the raised leg and stretch into a maximal arch. Turn the pelvis and shoulders as little as possible, chest opened as much as possible.
Cross version of the two-point support: the opposite arm reaches forward and up, the leg back and up. Maximal arch.
With the opposite hand, grip the ankle of the raised leg and stretch into an arch, trying not to turn the pelvis and shoulder girdle.
Slowly lower the pelvis onto the heels, toes extended, forehead on the floor, arms along the body. Relaxation.
Feet together, stand straight, palms joined in front of the chest. Relax and tune in to the round.
The arms rise overhead, a light backbend from the thoracic spine, head between the arms, pelvis slightly forward.
Bend forward from the pelvis with a long back, palms on the floor beside the feet; bend the knees slightly if needed. The forehead reaches toward the knees.
One leg goes far back, knee to the floor, front foot between the palms, shin vertical. Pelvis lowered, hands on the floor, chest open, gaze up.
Eight points of support: feet, knees, chest, chin and palms touch the floor, pelvis slightly raised, elbows pressed to the body.

Hands under the shoulders, elbows pressed to the sides. Pushing lightly with the arms, raise the chest, the neck and finally the head in a wave. The back does most of the work; the lower back lengthens, the pubic bone is pressed to the floor, sternum and head go straight up. Legs together, toes pointed, buttocks engaged.
From the lunge, without changing legs, raise the arms overhead and arch back into a crescent. Pelvis low, chest open.

From the plank, gently move the pelvis back onto the heels, the forehead lowers to the floor in front of the knees, the arms stay extended forward with palms on the floor. The back lengthens from the pelvis to the fingertips, shoulders free.

Wide horizontal plank: palms wide, fingers turned out; arms bent to a right angle, forearms vertical, elbows and shoulders in one line. In the rolls, the weight shifts right and left only horizontally, at least ten times.

Roll over the toes and lower the pelvis to the floor. The body reaches forward and up: navel forward, solar plexus forward and up, sternum and neck up, crown up and back. Shoulders back and down, legs together, buttocks engaged.
Lying on the belly, head turned to the side, arms relaxed along the body. An intermediate relaxation of no more than two or three minutes.

Lying on the belly, extend the arms forward, press with the palms and lift the head and shoulders, “crawling” the spine out of the pelvis. Navel pressed down, ribs “clinging” to the floor. Draw the wrists toward the shoulders, hands flexed toward you, head forward and up, straight legs back and up, toes pointed.

Elbows under the shoulders, shoulder-width apart, forearms parallel, fingers together and forward. Pushing with the forearms, lengthen the lower back forward, press the navel to the floor and lift the chest almost vertical. Legs together, toes pointed, buttocks engaged.
In the sphinx, without turning the pelvis, lift the straight leg as high as possible back and up, then lower it and repeat with the other leg.

Without changing the position of the hands, straighten the arms and lift the pelvis; the chest lowers toward the floor without the chin touching it. Neck long, sitting bones high, feet on the toes shoulder-width apart.
Pushing with the legs, lower the pelvis and reach forward again, now on straight arms. Legs together, toes pointed.
In the extended sphinx, bend one leg to the limit and lift the knee as high as possible, the pelvis does not turn. Then the other leg.

From the snake arch, turn the shoulders and head so that you see both heels over the shoulder. The head stays vertical, the pelvis still, the pubic bone pressed to the floor. Rotating the shoulders back and down opens the chest.

Pushing back with the arms, draw the torso away from the pelvis and arch to the limit, stretching the spine from tailbone to crown. Pubic bone on the floor, sternum up, neck up and back, head back and up.

From the snake arch, lift the pelvis, place the chin on the floor, put the feet on the toes; the hands stay in place. The spine reaches back and up, the palms of the straight arms joined, gaze forward.

With a smooth swing, take one arm out to the side and up, turning the shoulders; the other palm stays on the floor. Rest the back of the head on the supporting shoulder. The raised arm is strictly perpendicular to the body — this opens the chest and twists the straight spine.

Palms on the floor slightly wider than the shoulders, jump the legs about four shoulder-widths apart. Tilt the pelvis forward as far as possible, legs straight. Reach from the palms to the sitting bones: arms, back and pelvis in one plane. Gaze forward and down.
Without bending the arms, lower the pelvis and arch, stretching the body between heels and crown. Do not point the toes — the heels face up and reach back. Shoulders back and down, chest open.
Without tilting the pelvis or moving the legs, turn so that you see both feet with both eyes. Open the shoulders by rotating them back and down.
From the wide arched plank, stretch the crown up and bend the legs: knees on the floor and wide, feet together drawn toward the back. Maximal arch.

Feet on the toes, legs straight, pelvis raised as high as possible while keeping the arched plank position. The spine “curls” back: crown and tailbone draw toward each other, back muscles engaged to the limit.
A full arched plank, but without rolling over the toes: heels reach back, crown back and up, navel forward, sternum up. The body is stretched between heels and crown.
With a jump from the downward plank, tuck the legs and hang on straight arms without the feet touching the floor. Used as a transitional element.
Sitting, straight legs together extended forward, torso vertical, palms on the floor by the pelvis.
Lying on the back, legs loosely extended, arms slightly away from the body, palms up. Let the arms find a comfortable position on their own and relax completely, breathing freely.

Lying on the back, palms pressed to the floor. Pushing with the arms, swing the straight legs softly over the head until the toes touch the floor and return just as softly. Repeat ten to twelve times.

Lying on the back, take the straight arms through the sides behind the head, palms up, and press them to the floor. Legs together, toes pointed to the limit — the body stretched from fingertips to toes.
Relaxing the feet, slowly raise the straight legs to 30–35° and hold.
Slowly raise (or lower) the straight legs to an angle of about 60° and hold.
Legs vertical, toes flexed toward you to the limit, sacrum and tailbone pressed to the floor.

Arms to the sides. Slowly lower the rigidly straight legs to the side until the feet hover 15–20 cm above the palm; the head turns the opposite way. The spine is twisted but straight, the pelvis drawn back, heels pushed out.

Arms to the sides, place the foot of one leg on the knee of the other, shift the pelvis slightly and lower the knee to the floor, twisting the spine. Head turned away from the knee; shoulder blades, shoulders and elbows pressed to the floor.

Lying on the back, raise the straight legs vertically, then lower them behind the head and grip the feet with the palms. Legs straight, pull the feet toward you with the heels of the hands, and push the legs even farther by moving the pelvis.
Without releasing the feet, slowly bend the legs and place the knees on the floor by the ears, squeezing the head with the thighs.
Hands on the shins below the knees, back smoothly rounded. Do 7–8 gentle rolls from head to pelvis and back, without hitting the back of the head or the pelvis on the floor.

Feet by the pelvis, hands holding the ankles. Pushing the back off the floor, lift the pelvis and clearly draw the shoulder blades together. Weight on the shoulders and feet, arms straight, chest, solar plexus and lower belly open.

Keeping the chest open, slowly lower the pelvis to the floor. On the floor: back of the head, shoulders, elbows, sitting bones and feet; the neck and the whole back do not touch the floor. Back muscles engaged to the limit.
Legs and arms straight, hands in fists. With a firm push, arch the whole body into a tense arc, supported on the shoulders and heels. The knees do not bend.
Legs straight, hands one on top of the other under the neck, elbows out to the sides only for balance. With a push, arch the body into a rigid arc supported on the back of the head and the heels.

Hands interlocked, outer edges of the palms and elbows on the floor, elbows no wider than the shoulders. The head “fits” into the angle of the forearms. Slowly straighten the legs, raising the torso vertically; the feet are still on the floor.
Lean the torso back until the straight legs lift off the floor. Pelvis vertical, sitting bones high, straight legs rise to horizontal, toes toward you.

Extending at the hip joints, raise the straight legs and stretch vertically. The basic support according to the book is the point where the forehead meets the hairline; it is first learned on the crown. Usually 1–10 minutes; the author does not recommend more than 15–20 minutes.
In headstand, spread the knees apart and bend the legs, bringing the soles together.
In headstand, straighten the legs and spread them as wide as possible.
From the right angle, very slowly and with control, take the legs back. The arch is created by the back, the abs control speed and depth — no “free fall” of the legs.
From the half ring, gently tip back onto the feet. The legs straighten, the spine lengthens, feet shoulder-width apart; support on the head and feet.
In the head bridge, bend one leg and draw the knee as close to the chest as possible.
Straighten the bent leg vertically up, toes toward you.
Palms by the head; helping with the hands, roll onto the forehead, bending the legs slightly if needed. Place the hands on the thighs. Requires great attention to the neck.

Pressing with the palms, slowly lower the buttocks to the floor, trying to keep the head on the forehead rather than rolling onto the back of the head; the back arched to the limit. Extend the straight legs at an acute angle to the floor, toes toward you, straight arms parallel to the legs, palms facing each other.

Back, back of the head and neck pressed to the floor. Raise the legs and grip the big toes with “rings” made of the fingers. Legs rigidly straight, sacrum on the floor, shoulder blades pressed down; pull the toes toward you with the hands, draw the pelvis back.
Drawing the feet closer, place the palms on the soles and grip the heels with the fingers, pressing the toes with the forearms. Push the pelvis away from the head and fold in half at the hip joints.
Arms straight along the body, palms down, toes pointed, press the rigidly straight legs to the chest with all your strength.

With a smooth swing, straighten the whole body vertically up, placing the palms on the back closer to the shoulder blades. The support is the shoulders and upper arms, neck and head free; do not force the chin onto the chest. Elbows no wider than the shoulders.
Without changing the position of the torso and barely tilting the pelvis, slowly lower the straight legs behind the head until the pointed toes touch the floor.
Extend the straight arms back, join them in a reversed lock and press them to the floor. The spine reaches from the shoulders up to the tailbone, the crown away from the body. Toes toward you.
In shoulderstand, bend the legs, point the toes and lower the feet as far back as possible. Knees together, the fronts of the thighs and torso form one plane.
From the half shoulderstand, with a smooth swing, raise one leg vertically; the other stays with its toes on the floor behind the head.
Bend the raised leg to the limit, stretching the front of the thigh; the position of the torso and the other leg does not change.
From shoulderstand, arch back and place the feet on the floor. The palms support the back at kidney level, fingers out, elbows close; use the hands to lengthen the spine up from the shoulders.
In the supported shoulder bridge, straighten the legs, stretch their backs, toes toward you.
Without changing the body position, bend one leg and draw the knee to the chest; toes pointed.

Bending the legs slightly, turn the feet out; with a jump, kick the legs up and extend them vertically, soles horizontal. The key is the “step” at the pelvis: pelvis and belly horizontal, palms supporting the pelvis. The hold can be kept as long as you like.
Slowly lower the straight legs behind the head, arms in a reversed lock on the floor. Lengthen the spine by moving the feet away from the head; the pelvis tilts toward the feet, toes toward you.
Continuing to breathe evenly, point the toes and, by tilting the pelvis, push the feet even farther from the head.
Slowly, vertebra by vertebra, lower the back to the floor and place the arms in an open ring around the head — fingertips 2–3 cm apart. Complete relaxation.

Palms by the ears with fingers toward the shoulders, feet by the pelvis; the distance between the palms and between the feet is shoulder width. Stretching the body between the knees and elbows, lift the pelvis, back and head.

Straighten the arms and legs. The belly is like a tabletop, abs slightly engaged to protect the lower back. The depth of the backbend comes from opening the chest and shoulders, shoulder blades drawn together, feet parallel.
Pushing with the heels, straighten the legs and drop the head back, as if reaching the back of the head toward the tailbone. The lower back lengthens, the chest and shoulders open even more.
On the exhale, stretch even further, lift the head and draw the chin to the sternum.

Lying on the back, legs together and rigidly straight, toes toward you. Arms forward along the body, head and shoulders lift, chin to the jugular notch, lower back and sacrum pressed firmly to the floor.

Very slowly “curl” up into sitting, without a jerk at the critical point. Pull the buttocks out from under the sitting bones, tilt the pelvis forward, legs together and straight. Grip the feet, pull the toes toward you and stretch forward and up.

In a wave, lay the torso on the legs: first the belly, then the chest, the extended chin and the forehead. Pull the toes toward you with the heels of the hands, feet together, soles in one plane. Can be held as long as you like; in the start set usually 2–3 minutes.
Slowly and with tension draw the forehead to the navel, pressing the head firmly to the legs; push off the knees with the hands. The back opens like a hedgehog's, legs straight, toes toward you.
Palms by the hip joints, fingers toward the feet. In a wave, straighten the torso and, pushing with the arms, lift the pelvis until torso and thighs are horizontal. Shins vertical.
Bend the legs and shift the pelvis forward and down, letting it sag between the heels and stretching the fronts of the thighs. The arms rotate at the shoulders, the wrists stretch.

Palms on the floor behind, a forearm's length from the pelvis, fingers pointing away from the pelvis. In a wave, straighten the legs and stretch into an inclined plank facing up; pelvis as high as possible, toes pointed, do not throw the head back.
Bend the legs and shift the pelvis as far forward as possible, rotating the arms at the shoulders to the limit; the shoulder blades move back and down, opening the chest.
Lower the lower back to the floor, draw in the knees, straighten the legs and press the thighs to the belly; arms in the shoulder stretch.

Slowly tip onto the back, grip the heels and fold in half, toes toward you. Pressing on the heels, push the pelvis away from the head, spread the feet and push the head through between the legs, “looking past the pelvis”.
Standing on wide-apart straight legs, bend forward until the crown rests on the floor, hands holding the shins. The spine lengthens downward.
Palms on the floor, head raised, jump the feet forward, “landing” the knees on the shoulders.

Shift the weight back until the feet lift off and cross the ankles in front of you. Arms as straight as possible, knees do not slip off the shoulders, palms parallel. Ideally accumulate at least five minutes a day in total.
From the lock stance, straighten the legs out and up, toes pointed. A firm stand on straight arms with fully extended legs.

Lower the pelvis, bending the arms; place the feet, lie with the chest and belly on the floor and extend the arms to the sides. Straighten the legs, resting the calves on the forearms, toes toward you. Spread flat on the floor, heels off the floor.
Front view. Legs wide apart, hands holding the toes. Fold at the hip joints: belly, chest and chin to the floor as far from the pelvis as possible. Toes toward you, feet do not tip forward.
Front view. Hold the big toes with “rings” of the fingers and stretch forward and up, lifting the crown and arching back.

Front view. Turn the torso toward one leg without changing the position of the pelvis; the turn starts from the navel. Lay the belly and chest on the thigh, the chin reaching along the leg. Both sitting bones and both legs pressed to the floor.

Front view. Join the straight arms behind the back in a reversed lock, arch more strongly and lie into the bend, bringing the arms forward over the top. First the belly, then the chest, then the chin.
Front view. Rise with an arch, hands holding the thighs near the pelvis, back engaged to the limit, shoulders back and down, head back. Before coming out, hold on a full inhale for 15–20 seconds.

Front view. With a powerful exhale, swing the legs into a bend and bring the soles together at the perineum, knees wide. Hands interlocked at the belly, index fingers up, neck lock. Then breathe freely and feel the rising flow.
Front view. Take hold of the feet and press the “hearts” of the feet with the thumbs. With the exhale, direct the flow into the belly and close it with the root lock.

Front view. Without changing the position of the pelvis and feet, bend forward, pressing the “hearts” of the feet to the solar plexus; chest and chin on the floor. In the “hedgehog” version the back rounds, crown to the feet.

Front leg straight, on the heel far forward, back leg straight and on the toes; both feet vertical. Pelvis “square” — perpendicular to the legs. With each exhale the pelvis sags lower. Front heel forward, back heel back, crown forward and up.
In a wave, lay the torso on the front thigh, the hand pulls the toes toward you. Weight on the back toes and front heel, keeping the pelvis square.

On a slow exhale, release the back toes and lay the back leg on the floor along its whole front surface. The torso slides to the floor, chin as far forward as possible. Relax, keeping the pelvis level.
Front splits: in a wave, lift the torso, lengthen the spine up and arch back.
From the splits, in a soft wave, lower into the extended bend toward the front leg.

Front view. Knees wide, move the calves out from under the knees with the hands and lower the pelvis to the floor between the heels. The big toes touch. Pull the buttocks out, tilt the pelvis forward, palms of the straight arms on the knees.
Front view. One hand reaches behind the back to hold the thigh, the other holds the opposite knee; turn the shoulders and head to the limit; pelvis still, spine straight.
Front view. Hands interlocked, arms up, turn the lock out and arch, stretching the neck forward and up. Pelvis tilted forward, shoulder blades down, chest open.
Front view. Palms on the feet, in a wave lay the torso on the floor: pelvis, belly, chest and chin. In the “hedgehog” version the back rounds, the forehead reaching toward the navel.
Kneeling, raise the arms up through the sides and arch back, smoothly lifting the pelvis.
Straighten up on the knees, arms extended up.
Pelvis on the floor between the feet, knees together, feet pointing back and parallel. Pull the buttocks out, pelvis slightly forward, spine straight, shoulders open. Backs of the hands on the knees.
Hands behind the back in a reversed lock, raise the straight arms as high as possible; the head lowers, chin to the jugular notch.
Lock in front, arms up with the lock turned out. Pelvis forward, shoulders back, neck forward and up — a half arch, as in the basic stance.
Holding the half arch, spread the arms to the sides with tension, as if pushing two walls apart.
Palms on the feet, in a wave lay the torso on the thighs; chin to the floor, then neck lock and forehead to the floor. Relaxation.
Sliding the forehead and crown along the thighs, round the back and draw the forehead toward the navel.

In a wave, straighten up, move the pelvis forward and up and stretch into a backbend; knees shoulder-width apart, palms on the feet. The body is the bow, the arms are the string. Do not throw the head back: it continues the line of the neck.
Kneeling, straight arms forward and swing up; the neck lengthens back, but the back of the head does not press to the back.
With a smooth swing, take the arms back.
Continuing the circular movement, place the palms on the thighs and, fixing the distance from the shoulders to the pelvis with the arms, deepen the backbend as if to close the spine into a ring.

Holding the thighs, very slowly lean back until the head reaches the floor, then take hold of the toes or heels. The backbend is mostly thoracic; always keep some reserve in the lower back. Knees and elbows no wider than the shoulders.
Release the feet, palms on the floor roughly where the elbows were, fingers toward the feet. Straighten the arms, the wrists stretch strongly.
From virasana, lower the back to the floor, knees together, relax.
Take hold of the ankles and arch up, drawing the crown toward the pelvis. Head and pelvis on the floor, back and neck off the floor, thighs squeezed together.
Cross the forearms in front of the chest and take the arms behind the head, reaching the elbows toward the floor. Chest fully open.

Palms on the heels, back on the floor. Lift the head and shoulders, straightening and pressing down the lower back; push off the heels with the hands. In the side version, the upper body turns, stretching the opposite side.
Continuing to press the lower back down, raise the knees and head toward each other, as if curling into a ring. The front of the body is engaged.

Palms between the thighs with fingers toward the perineum, elbows together pressing into the navel. Lean forward, lying with the belly on the elbows, straighten the legs back and lift them; arch back with the abs engaged. The elbows do not splay.
Bend the legs and relax the belly slightly, letting the elbows “sink in”. Alternate with straight legs.
Feet shoulder-width apart, hands under the feet. In a wave, lay the torso on the thighs, pull the spine down with the arms and push the head through between the knees.
Bend the knees until the back is almost horizontal. On the inhale, elbows back, open palms by the thighs facing forward; then on the hold — fists, elbows to the thighs, the whole body tense.
On the exhale, hands interlocked and forward on straight arms, index fingers together — sampurna mudra.
Raise the torso vertically, thighs strictly horizontal, standing on the whole foot. The torso does not tip forward.
Rise onto the toes as high as possible, thighs still horizontal; slowly spread the arms to the sides or extend them forward wrists first, hands flexed toward you.
Sharply and fully draw the elbows back and pull the hands to the torso.
In the open bend, continuing the shoulder stretch, round the back and draw the forehead toward the perineum; the head goes up between the legs.
Front view. Feet together, straight arms slowly spread to the sides, shoulders broad, shoulder blades pressed to the back, chest open.
Front view. Hands behind the back: one from above, the other from below; the hands join on the spine by the shoulder blades in a “bear lock”. Shoulders broad, upper elbow up. Bend to the side.
With the “bear lock” behind the back, bend forward on straight legs, the spine reaching down.
Front view. Cross the arms twice and wrap the forearms, palms together. In the same way “wrap” one leg around the other and squat, placing the foot on the instep of the supporting one.
Straighten the arms and legs as much as possible, stretching strongly upward. After coming out, do not relax; observe the wave of sensations.
Horse stance: feet 1.5–2 shoulder-widths apart, parallel. Palms joined between the shoulder blades. Leaning slightly at the hips, lengthen the spine and arch, shoulders back and down.
Straight arms on the fronts of the thighs; arch even more, without a kink in the lower back.
Arms forward, up and behind the head, the knees bend — preparing to lower into the bridge.
In the bridge, lift one leg and place the same-side hand on the thigh. Then mirrored.
Bend the arms, lower the elbows to the floor and bring the feet in so that the heels are between the hands — a bridge on the forearms.
Forearm scorpion: “crawl” the spine through between the arms, arching more but without a kink. The legs bend loosely, feet hanging over the head.
In the scorpion, extend first one leg up, then the other.
Feet on the floor, crown on the floor, palms shoulder-width apart, elbows over the palms, legs straight.
Smoothly raise the straight legs and stretch into a headstand supported on the palms; support on the crown.
In headstand, fold the legs into lotus: first one foot onto the base of the opposite thigh, then the other.
Transitional position: head on the floor, the lotus resting on the arm by the armpit.
Side rooster: turn the pelvis, place the lotus thigh on the arm by the armpit, straighten the arms and come into a handstand with torso and legs horizontal.

Very slowly and carefully lower the pelvis until the spine is vertical; the pelvis hovers a few centimetres above the floor. A maximal twist with traction from the body weight — requires strict discipline.
The shins of the crossed legs rest on the arm by the armpit; straightening the arms, come into a handstand. Then mirrored.
In headstand, fold at the hips and press the lotus to the belly, the shins resting in the armpits.
Lower the pelvis and, as it were, sit the thighs on the elbows; lotus horizontal.
Straighten the arms, raise the head, lotus pressed to the belly, the pelvis lowers. Hold as long as your training allows.
From rooster, lift the pelvis and knees and stretch into a vertical stand on straight arms with lotus.
Vertical stand on straight arms, body extended, unnecessary muscles relaxed. Do not rush.
In handstand, reach the head forward and up, “threading” the torso between the arms; the legs bend and hang over the head. A ring from toes to crown, no kink in the lower back.
In the scorpion, extend one leg vertically up, then the other.
From the pyramid fold take the left ankle with the right hand, raise the left arm and twist; then the other side.
From the wide bend, push the head and shoulders through between the legs and, pushing with the shoulders, as it were wrap the torso around the pelvis.
Shins on the shoulders, ankles crossed on the back of the head; push up and stand on the hands with the legs folded behind the head for as long as possible.
Thread the head through between the shins and lower the ankle lock in front of you to the level of the solar plexus; then change the lock.
Tuck stance: arms straight, heels drawn to the buttocks, toes pointed. Back as straight and long as possible, pelvis lowered, head raised. While holding, perform the “metal dog breath”.
Place the supporting foot under the middle of the pelvis on the toes, stretch and raise the other leg vertically.
With a short jump, bring the feet right up to the hands; belly horizontal, arms vertical, chest open.
Slowly, with strength only, rise to standing and join the hands in front of the chest — sampurna mudra, the “symbol of the completed flow”.
In the seated bend, bring the arms behind the back, join them in a reversed lock and perform a deep shoulder stretch.
Sliding the head along the legs, draw the forehead toward the navel, the arms stay in the shoulder stretch.
Front view. In the half-splits bend, join the palms between the shoulder blades, pressing the heels of the hands firmly together.

Front view. Hands on the knees, chin to the jugular notch. A “pumping” exhale into the belly, root lock; then on the hold — abdominal lock (draw the belly in) or abdominal churn (a ridge of the rectus muscles), 10–20 seconds each. The inhale afterward is smooth.

Front view. Press one heel to the perineum below the navel, place the other foot on top, tucking the toes between the calf and thigh. Backs of the hands on the legs, one on top of the other, thumbs touching. Spine straight — a pose for Breath and Contemplation of Power.
From the snake arch, bend the leg and with the same-side hand grip the instep from below: palm up, thumb toward the ankle. Rotating the arm, raise the elbow and draw the foot to the forehead.
Slowly bend the supporting arm until the lower chest rests on the floor; take the foot with the other hand too and draw it to the forehead with both hands.
Place the forearm of the free arm on the floor; pushing with the supporting leg, lift the pelvis and lay the forehead on the forearm, still holding the foot.
Release the foot and extend the leg up, toes toward you; hands one on top of the other, chin on the hands.
Straighten the arm and slowly turn the pelvis, reaching the raised foot toward the opposite elbow. Upper chest and shoulders pressed to the floor.
From the arched plank on the toes, lower the knees, bend the legs and, broadening the shoulders, curl into a ring, trying to reach the toes with the forehead.
In headstand, describe two horizontal semicircles with the legs, opening into front half splits; the pelvis turns to the limit.

In headstand, fold the legs into lotus without using the hands: take one leg back, place the other foot in its crease, then the second foot. Align the pelvis and lotus vertically; in the variations, turn the lotus right and left.
With the spine extended vertically, fold at the hips and press the lotus to the belly; in the “hedgehog” version the shins go into the armpits.
From headstand with lotus, push strongly with the arms and come into forearm stand; maximal arch, head raised, palms together, elbows no wider than the shoulders.
In forearm stand, straighten the legs and stretch into an arch; palms parallel, elbows do not splay.
Along a ring-shaped path, reach the forehead toward the tailbone; the feet come to the hands, and the hands hold the ankles. Forearms parallel if possible.
Forearm stand with straight legs vertically up. In the “reverse” exit, the legs rise only with a slow strength movement, no swinging.
In Viparita Karani, fold the legs into lotus: one foot onto the base of the opposite thigh, then the other, shins crossed.

Fold at the hips, pressing the lotus to the belly and chest; place the knees on the floor by the head and wrap the legs with the arms in a wrist lock. In the side version the knees go to the side of the head. Weight on the shoulders and knees.
Press the arms to the floor, then bring the palms under the back, elbows close. Stretch vertically into shoulderstand with lotus.
Arms in a reversed lock behind the back, lower the knees to the floor behind the head. Dangerous for the neck: only with the shoulder stretch, smoothly and without jerks.
From shoulderstand with lotus, turn the pelvis and lower it to the side, arching in the lower back and supporting it with the hands.
Slowly bend the legs and place the knees on the floor as far behind the head as possible. Same precautions as in the lotus plough.
Pushing with the arms, stretch vertically into shoulderstand and join the hands behind the back in a reversed lock.
Lift the arms and extend them along the body — shoulderstand without support. Stand on the shoulders, not on the neck and back of the head.
Pelvis tilted slightly forward, palms pressed together between the shoulder blades. Arch the torso, open the chest, head back, press the base of the skull with the middle fingers.
Straight arms on the thighs; lengthening the spine, arch back until the sternum is horizontal.
In the locked elbow bridge, release one leg and extend it up, toes toward you, hand on the floor.
Swing the legs to the floor and come into an open bend: torso and arms extended so that the fingers barely touch the floor; legs straight, feet parallel.
Palms on the floor, shift the weight onto the arms until the legs lift off; stretch the torso up and slowly raise the straight legs to horizontal.
From the reverse half plank, straighten the legs and lift the pelvis as high as possible, folding in half; belly to the thighs, face between the shins. In the open version, feet shoulder-width apart.
Lower the pelvis, straighten the legs and hold them in front of you parallel to the floor; heels off the floor, support on the arms.
Front view. Press the hands into the floor behind the pelvis, lift the pelvis and shift it forward, pressing the lower belly to the feet. Knees lower. Requires very advanced preparation.

Front view. The feet turn out with the heels forward and lie on their sides on the floor, the perineum over the feet, hands in front on the fingertips. Neck and root locks, hold on the inhale, then exhale and jump into the horizontal plank.
In the front splits, bend the back leg, thread the same-side arm under the foot, raise the elbow and place the foot on the crown, toes toward the forehead. The other hand holds the floor.
In the reverse half plank, extend one leg up.
Place the foot of the raised leg on the base of the opposite thigh, bring the knees closer, thighs in one horizontal plane.

Sit down, pull the buttocks out, tilt the pelvis forward. One leg in half lotus, thigh pressed to the floor; the hands, one on top of the other, press the toes of the extended leg, foot vertical. Straight spine forward and up.
In a wave, lay the torso on the thighs, pull the foot of the extended leg toward you. Knees together, the half-lotus thigh on the floor.
Stretch forward and up and, reaching behind the back with the same-side hand, grip the foot resting on the thigh. The shoulder girdle does not turn.
With the half lotus locked, lie down on the thighs in a wave, the chin reaching forward; shoulders in one horizontal plane.
Sitting in half lotus, stretch and turn, reaching behind the back to grip the shin of the half lotus; the other hand holds the foot of the straight leg. The head turns too, gaze back, spine straight.

Front view. The feet rest on the opposite thighs at the creases, shins crossed, knees on the floor. Spine vertical, torso relaxed, hands on the crossed shins. Close the eyes for a few breathing cycles.
Front view. One hand reaches behind the back to grip the shin, the other rests on the opposite knee, deepening the turn; head turned to the limit, gaze back, spine vertical.
Front view. Hands on the knees, neck long, chin to the chest. Slowly rotate the head with maximum range — the same number of rotations in each direction.
Front view. In lotus, interlock the hands, turn the lock out and reach up, “lifting the sky” with the palms. Pelvis forward, shoulders back, chest open.
Front view. Lock behind the back, palms out; in a wave from the pelvis, lay the torso on the floor, chin as far forward as possible. The straight arms rise up and reach forward.

Front view. Reaching behind the back, each hand grips the foot on the same side (the big toe in a “ring”), then straighten up and open the chest. Variations: the reverse order of the grip and arms crossed at the elbows. Can be held for an unlimited time.

Front view. After the “metal dog” and the hold with locks, bend forward in a wave, touching the floor with the chin, belly on the lotus. Then forehead past the right knee, then past the left — always to the right first.
Releasing the feet, roll over the knees: pelvis raised, chest on the floor; grip the feet again from behind the back.
Reach the chin forward, lift the head as high as possible and lower the pelvis, pressing the lotus feet to the floor.
Chin on the floor, palms joined between the shoulder blades.
Reach the chin forward and arch back to the limit, palms between the shoulder blades.
Palms under the shoulders, reach forward, “crawling” the torso out of the pelvis; belly pressed down, ribs “clinging” to the floor. Legs in lotus.

Palms where the elbows were, arms straight, the body sagging between the shoulders and knees. A deep inhale; tongue to the chest, eyes to the point between the eyebrows, root lock and a powerful exhale through the mouth with the sound “ha”. Then a slow inhale through the mouth. Repeat several times.
Shoulders back, both hands grip the shins where they cross, and arch to the limit.
Palms under the groin, fingers back, forearms together, elbows into the belly. Lift the head and legs, one leg straightened back, the other in half lotus. Hold for at least a minute.
Bend one leg and grip the foot from below, elbow up, foot to the head. Thread the other arm through the “ring” and grip the half-lotus foot. Head straight.
Release the feet, legs in lotus, arms extended forward — relaxation lying on the belly.
Roll over the knees, the pelvis rises, lotus almost vertical. Elbows on the floor, head in the palms, a relaxed, free backbend.
Front view. Bend in free lotus: forehead to the floor, arms forward, palms together. In the “hedgehog” version, hands hold the knees, the head reaches toward the perineum, back rounded.
Front view. Bend in lotus, chin to the floor, palms joined between the shoulder blades. In the variations, the torso shifts right and left toward the knees or twists with the shoulder past the knee.
Palms on the floor behind the pelvis, fingers back, slightly wider than the shoulders. Pelvis forward, shoulders broad, chest open.
Pushing with the arms, lift the pelvis and arch, head back; the neck lengthens rather than kinks.

Arms up to the elbows through the gaps between the thighs and shins, lotus pressed to the belly, hands in sampurna mudra; balance on the buttocks. Variation: wrap the lotus with the arms from the outside.
Palms (fingertips, fists) at the sides of the pelvis, rise on the arms, holding the lotus suspended in front of you.
From the lifted lotus, straighten the legs in front of you and balance on the arms as long as possible.

From Paschimottanasana, reach one arm to the opposite knee, “hooking” it with the armpit, extend the other arm up and look at its thumb. Then hold the feet crosswise and twist even more along the legs.
From the deep downward plank, with a soft jump, place the knees at the armpits — just outside, as if hooking the thighs onto the shoulders. Arms slightly bent, feet tucked.
From the tuck stance, one leg straightens forward. At first you may lightly support your balance with the big toe of the supporting leg.
Without changing the position of the supporting knee, bend the extended leg and take it back with a soft swing. Try to bring the body almost horizontal.

The supporting foot is placed between the palms and the leg straightens fully. The other leg bends, the heel reaching toward the buttock, the knee toward the middle of the back. The forehead presses to the straight leg and slides toward the navel, the back rounds like a curled-up hedgehog. Abs contracted to the limit.
Half arch in the extended bend on one leg: palms on the floor, the back arches while the free leg reaches as far back and up as possible.

One hand holds the ankle of the supporting leg, the other presses into the floor. The free leg reaches ever higher, the chin slides along the supporting leg toward the foot. Navel to the thigh, sitting bones up, the pelvis does not turn.

Both hands on the floor slightly in front of the supporting foot, chin pressed down — neck lock. Bend the raised leg and throw the foot behind the back, turning the pelvis as far as possible and opening the groin.

The pelvis returns to a square position, the free leg goes straight up again. With a circular swing, bring the straight arms behind the back into a reversed lock and, using them as a lever, pull the shoulders down.

Balancing on the straight supporting leg, extend the torso forward and arch, raising the head high; the pelvis barely rises. The free leg bends, the toes reaching toward the crown. On the inhale, pull the hands to the sides — an inhale “from the earth” into the solar plexus.

Quickly straighten up leaning slightly back, raising the knee of the free leg and drawing the foot toward the perineum, toes pointed. The arms sharply straighten forward and down, hands flexed toward you; a firm full exhale “through the palms”, as if pushing off the earth.

On the inhale, lean back, the free leg straightens horizontally forward, toes pointed. With bent fingers, as if drawing an invisible stream under the back. The solar plexus is the highest point of the torso.
On the exhale, straighten up and place the free leg as far back as possible — a wide step. The arms straighten forward and down again, “pushing the earth” with the centres of the palms.

In the wide step with the knee on the floor, bend the back leg. One hand holds the floor, the other reaches from behind the head to grip the foot and, lengthening the spine, arch until the crown touches the foot. The lines of the shoulders and pelvis are parallel and perpendicular to the body.
Continuing the ring: thread the head under the elbow and draw the foot from behind to the opposite shoulder.

Press the instep of the back foot with the hand, pressing it to the pelvis. Bring the opposite shoulder past the front thigh, hand on the floor, and, pushing with the shoulder, strongly twist the lengthened spine; the head turns to the limit in the direction of the twist. The pelvis lowers forward and down, stretching the thigh.
Cross ring: grip the back foot from behind the head with the opposite hand and, using the back muscles, press the crown to the foot. Level the pelvis and shoulder girdle.
The head threads under the elbow, the foot is drawn from behind to the shoulder on the same side as the leg.

With the same-side hand, press firmly on the toes and instep of the back leg, pressing the heel from the side to the hip joint. The other hand rests on the front knee, then lay the torso on the front thigh and push the heel down even harder.
Pushing off the front thigh with the hand, lengthen the spine and arch back, continuing to press on the back foot. The pelvis lowers, the perineum and the front of the thigh stretch even more.

Releasing the leg, bring the same-side hand under the foot from the outside: palm up, thumb toward the ankle. Grip the foot from below and, rotating the arm at the shoulder, raise the elbow up. Keep the head straight — the way a camel proudly carries its head. Pelvis and shoulders level.
With the same-side hand, press the toes to the shoulder joint from behind and above. The arch is held more by the back muscles than by the grip.
The same as the extended one-sided camel, but the foot is held with the opposite hand.
With the opposite hand, draw the foot to the head, pressing the toes to the opposite shoulder if possible. Do not throw the head back.
